summary.text: Choose the least time \(d\) at which the Collatz trajectory of a given positive integer reaches \(1\), and induct backward along these \(d\) steps. An even predecessor \(w\) is recovered as the halving child \(2(w/2)\), while an odd predecessor \(w\ne1\) makes \(3w+1>4\) a branching node with \(6\mid(3w+3)\) and is recovered as \(((3w+1)-1)/3\); choosing the corresponding branch bits at each stage yields an encoding from the root to the original integer.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C(x)=\begin{cases}
x/2,&x\text{ even},\\
3x+1,&x\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\]
be the Collatz map on the nonnegative integers. Write \(C^j\) for its \(j\)-fold iterate, with \(C^0(x)=x\).

We first restate precisely the decoding operation defining the sequence. For nonnegative integers \(r,v\), let \(F(r,v)\) denote the result of starting the decoding procedure with code \(r\) at a node whose value is \(v\). Thus \(F\) is determined recursively as follows.

* If \(r=0\), then
  \[
  F(0,v)=v.
  \]
* Suppose \(r>0\), and put \(s=r-1\). Call \(v\) a branching value when
  \[
  v>4\qquad\text{and}\qquad v+2\equiv0\pmod 6.
  \]
  If \(v\) is not branching, then
  \[
  F(r,v)=F(s,2v).
  \]
  If \(v\) is branching, then
  \[
  F(r,v)=
  \begin{cases}
  F(s/2,2v),&s\text{ even},\\
  F(\lfloor s/2\rfloor,(v-1)/3),&s\text{ odd}.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Here all quotients are integer quotients; in the branching condition, \((v-1)/3\) is in fact an integer, since \(v+2\) being divisible by \(6\) implies in particular that \(v\equiv1\pmod3\).

The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=F(n,1).
\]

We shall prove the following reversal lemma, which is the main part of the argument.

**Reversal lemma.** Let \(m>0\) and let \(d\geq0\). Suppose that
\[
C^i(m)\ne1\qquad(0\leq i<d).
\]
Then there is a nonnegative integer \(r\) such that
\[
F\bigl(r,C^d(m)\bigr)=m.
\]

In words, if the first \(d\) positions before time \(d\) on the Collatz trajectory avoid \(1\), then one can encode, starting at the node \(C^d(m)\), the reverse path back to \(m\).

Before proving the lemma, note that every iterate \(C^i(m)\) is positive when \(m>0\). Indeed, \(C\) preserves positivity: if a positive \(x\) is odd, then \(C(x)=3x+1>0\); if it is even, then a positive even integer is at least \(2\), so \(C(x)=x/2\geq1\). Induction on \(i\) now gives positivity of every iterate.

We prove the reversal lemma by induction on \(d\).

For \(d=0\), take \(r=0\). Since \(C^0(m)=m\), the stopping rule for the decoder gives
\[
F(0,C^0(m))=F(0,m)=m.
\]

Now suppose the lemma is known for \(d\), and consider the case \(d+1\). Set
\[
w=C^d(m),\qquad v=C(w)=C^{d+1}(m).
\]
The avoidance hypothesis for times less than \(d+1\) implies both that the earlier iterates avoid \(1\) for times less than \(d\), and that
\[
w\ne1.
\]
By the induction hypothesis, there is some \(q\geq0\) such that
\[
F(q,w)=m. \tag{1}
\]
It remains to construct a code which, when started at \(v=C(w)\), first moves from \(v\) to its child \(w\), and then continues with code \(q\). We split according to the parity of \(w\).

### Case 1: \(w\) is even

Then
\[
v=C(w)=w/2.
\]
Since \(w\) is even, this gives
\[
2v=w. \tag{2}
\]
There are two subcases, depending on whether \(v\) satisfies the decoder’s branching criterion.

If \(v\) is not branching, choose
\[
r=q+1.
\]
This is positive, and after the decoder decrements \(r\), its residual code is exactly \(q\). At a nonbranching value it moves to the sole child \(2v\). Therefore, using (2) and then (1),
\[
F(q+1,v)=F(q,2v)=F(q,w)=m.
\]

If \(v\) is branching, choose instead
\[
r=2q+1.
\]
After decrementing this code, the residual value is \(2q\), which is even. The branching rule therefore chooses the doubling child \(2v\), and divides the residual code by \(2\), leaving \(q\). Consequently,
\[
F(2q+1,v)=F(q,2v)=F(q,w)=m.
\]
Thus the desired code exists in either subcase.

### Case 2: \(w\) is odd

We know that \(w>0\), and the avoidance hypothesis gave \(w\ne1\). Hence a positive odd \(w\) must satisfy
\[
w\geq3. \tag{3}
\]
In this case
\[
v=C(w)=3w+1. \tag{4}
\]
We claim that \(v\) is a branching value. First, (3) and (4) imply
\[
v=3w+1\geq10>4.
\]
Second,
\[
v+2=3w+3=3(w+1).
\]
Because \(w\) is odd, \(w+1\) is even, so \(3(w+1)\) is divisible by \(6\). Thus \(v+2\equiv0\pmod6\), proving the branching claim. Notice that this is exactly where the condition \(w\ne1\) matters: if \(w=1\), then \(v=4\), which is deliberately excluded from the branching nodes by the requirement \(v>4\).

Now choose
\[
r=2q+2.
\]
After decrementing, the residual code is \(2q+1\), which is odd. Since \(v\) is branching, the decoder therefore takes the tripling-step child and changes the code to
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2q+1}{2}\right\rfloor=q.
\]
Moreover, by (4),
\[
\frac{v-1}{3}=\frac{3w}{3}=w.
\]
It follows from the branching recursion and (1) that
\[
F(2q+2,v)=F\left(q,\frac{v-1}{3}\right)=F(q,w)=m.
\]

This completes both parity cases and hence the induction, proving the reversal lemma.

We can now prove the conjectured consequence. Assume the Collatz conjecture: for every positive integer \(m\), there is some \(k\geq0\) for which
\[
C^k(m)=1.
\]
Fix an arbitrary positive integer \(m\). Among all indices at which its trajectory reaches \(1\), choose the least one, say \(d\). Then
\[
C^d(m)=1, \tag{5}
\]
and by minimality,
\[
C^i(m)\ne1\qquad\text{for every }i<d. \tag{6}
\]
Apply the reversal lemma to \(m\) and this least index \(d\). It supplies a nonnegative integer \(r\) such that
\[
F(r,C^d(m))=m.
\]
Using (5), this becomes
\[
F(r,1)=m.
\]
But by definition \(a(r)=F(r,1)\). Therefore
\[
a(r)=m.
\]
Since \(m>0\) was arbitrary, every positive integer occurs among the values of the sequence \(a(n)\), as claimed.
